section.title: The Prayer Against the Accuser
section.sectionRationale: One of the fiercest imprecatory psalms, this prayer of a slandered man entrusts vengeance entirely to God rather than taking it into his own hands, and its language concerning the wicked man's office is later applied by the apostles to Judas Iscariot.
section.thesis: When love is repaid with hatred and lies, the godly response is not private revenge but honest lament that hands the accuser over to God's justice, resting all hope of rescue on the LORD's steadfast love alone.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the cry against slander, verses 1-5; the imprecation against the accuser, verses 6-20; the psalmist's own frailty and plea, verses 21-25; the prayer for public vindication, verses 26-29; and the closing vow of praise, verses 30-31.

verses.text: For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. O God of my praise, be not silent.
For wicked and deceitful mouths open against me; they speak against me with lying tongues.
They surround me with hateful words and attack me without cause.
In return for my love they accuse me, but I am a man of prayer.
They repay me evil for good, and hatred for my love.

units.label: The prayer against the accuser
units.note: imprecation entrusted to God, applied to Judas' office in Acts 1:20

verses.text: Set over him a wicked man; let an {{satan|accuser}} stand at his right hand.
When he is tried, let him be found guilty, and may his prayer be regarded as sin.
May his days be few; may another take his position.
May his children be fatherless and his wife a widow.
May his children wander as beggars, seeking sustenance far from their ruined homes.
May the creditor seize all he owns, and strangers plunder the fruits of his labor.
May there be no one to extend kindness to him, and no one to favor his fatherless children.
May his descendants be cut off; may their name be blotted out from the next generation.
May the iniquity of his fathers be remembered before the LORD, and the sin of his mother never be blotted out.
May their sins always remain before the LORD, that He may cut off their memory from the earth.
For he never thought to show kindness, but pursued the poor and needy and brokenhearted, even to their death.
The cursing that he loved, may it fall on him; the blessing in which he refused to delight, may it be far from him.
The cursing that he wore like a coat, may it soak into his body like water, and into his bones like oil.
May it be like a robe wrapped about him, like a belt tied forever around him.
May this be the LORD's reward to my accusers, to those who speak evil against me.
But You, O GOD, the Lord, deal kindly with me for the sake of Your name; deliver me by the goodness of Your {{chesed|loving devotion}}.
For I am poor and needy; my heart is wounded within me.
I am fading away like a lengthening shadow; I am shaken off like a locust.
My knees are weak from fasting, and my body grows lean and gaunt.
I am an object of scorn to my accusers; when they see me, they shake their heads.

units.label: A plea for public vindication
units.note: let them know this is Your hand

verses.text: Help me, O LORD my God; save me according to Your loving devotion.
Let them know that this is Your hand, that You, O LORD, have done it.
Though they curse, You will bless. When they rise up, they will be put to shame, but Your servant will rejoice.
May my accusers be clothed with disgrace; may they wear their shame like a robe.

units.label: A vow of praise
units.note: He stands at the right hand of the needy

verses.text: With my mouth I will thank the LORD profusely; I will praise Him in the presence of many.
For He stands at the right hand of the needy one, to save him from the condemners of his soul.

satan.gloss: An adversary or accuser, often in a legal setting standing at a defendant's side to bring charges. David asks that the accuser's own tactic, false accusation, be turned back on him in a just courtroom reversal.

chesed.gloss: Steadfast, covenant love and loyalty. David's entire hope for rescue, both from slander and from harm, rests not on his own righteousness but on God's chesed alone, verses 21 and 26.

basic.context: David is surrounded by liars who repay his love and prayers with hatred and false accusation. Rather than taking revenge himself, he hands his accuser over to God in the fiercest imprecatory language in the Psalter, then turns to confess his own frailty and beg for rescue.
basic.hermeneutics: The curses are not personal vindictiveness but a legal appeal, asking the righteous Judge to let the accuser's own schemes fall back on his own head, a pattern of justice repeatedly affirmed elsewhere in Scripture. Peter later reads verse 8 as prophetic of Judas' office being filled by another, Acts 1:20.
basic.originalLanguages: David asks that a satan, an accuser, stand at his enemy's right hand in the same way accusers stood in Israel's courts, verse 6, a reversal of what has been done to him. His only appeal for rescue in verses 21 and 26 is God's chesed, His steadfast covenant love, not any merit of his own.
basic.typology: David, the anointed but falsely accused king, foreshadows Christ, who was falsely accused before Caiaphas and Pilate yet entrusted Himself to the Father who judges justly; the wicked accuser of this psalm anticipates Judas, whose betrayal of the greater David is explicitly read through this psalm in Acts 1:20.
basic.christ: Jesus, like David, was hated in return for love and falsely accused by wicked and deceitful mouths, yet He did not revile in return but entrusted Himself to God who judges justly, 1 Peter 2:23. Peter applies this psalm's language of the accuser's office being filled by another directly to Judas Iscariot, Acts 1:20, showing that the psalm's justice reaches even to the betrayer of the true Son of David.
basic.god: God is the righteous Judge who alone has the right to repay evil, so David surrenders his case entirely into God's hand rather than seizing vengeance himself. God is also gracious and near to the poor and needy, standing at the right hand of the very needy one this psalm portrays, ready to save him from his condemners.
basic.crossReferences: Acts 1:20 quotes verse 8 directly of Judas' replacement in the apostolic office. Romans 12:19 commands believers to leave vengeance to God rather than repay evil for evil. 1 Peter 2:23 shows Christ's own pattern of entrusting Himself to the Father rather than retaliating under false accusation.
basic.oneStory: A falsely accused servant of God hands his case entirely to the righteous Judge rather than seizing vengeance himself; this pattern reaches its full weight in Christ, who was hated for His love, and whose betrayer, Judas, is judged by the very words of this psalm, while the true King is finally vindicated and saved by the God who stands at the right hand of the needy.

context.literary:
The psalm has the three-part shape of a lament, complaint, petition and vow, but it distorts the proportions on purpose. The central block of verses 6 to 20 is a single sustained curse, fifteen verses long, and it is flanked by two much shorter movements: the opening complaint of verses 1 to 5 and a personal plea of verses 21 to 29. The vow of verses 30 and 31 is only two verses. The reader is meant to feel the weight of the middle.

Three threads tie the poem together. The first is the accuser. The Hebrew root behind 'satan' runs through the psalm: the enemies 'accuse' the speaker in verse 4, an 'accuser' is set at the enemy's right hand in verse 6, and the speaker's own 'accusers' are named in verses 20 and 29. What the enemies do to David is what David asks to be done to the chief enemy.

The second is clothing. The enemy 'wore' cursing 'like a coat' and is to be wrapped in it 'like a robe' and 'a belt,' verses 18 and 19, and the speaker's accusers are in turn to be 'clothed with disgrace' and to 'wear their shame like a robe,' verse 29. The image brackets the whole of the prayer: what a person puts on, he will have to wear.

The third is the right hand. In verse 6 the accuser stands 'at his right hand,' the place of prosecution. In the last verse, the LORD 'stands at the right hand of the needy one,' the place of defence. The same words mark the first and last movement of the psalm's argument, and the psalm ends where the curse began, with a reversal.

A fourth link joins the victims to the speaker. The wicked man 'pursued the poor and needy and brokenhearted,' verse 16, and the speaker then says, 'I am poor and needy; my heart is wounded within me,' verse 22. The man who has been hunted is among those the enemy hunts, and the curse is therefore an appeal to the God who defends such people.
context.historical:
The title assigns the psalm to David, and the situation is a courtroom of public opinion. The language of verses 2 to 5 is of mouths, tongues and words, and verses 6 and 7 use trial language: someone is 'set over him,' he is 'tried' and 'found guilty.' In ancient Israel a person accused of a crime stood before the elders at the gate, and a hostile witness would stand beside him to press the charge. Where a malicious witness was caught, the law gave him the punishment he had intended, Deuteronomy 19:18 and 19. The prayer asks God to apply that principle.

The sins named in verse 16 also have a legal background. The wicked man did not show loyal kindness, chesed, to the poor, and pursued them to their death. The curses in verses 9 to 12 mirror penalties the law attached to oppressing the vulnerable. In Exodus 22:22 to 24 God warns anyone who mistreats a widow or orphan that He will hear their cry and that the oppressor's wives will become widows and his children fatherless. The images of verses 9 and 10 are therefore not original to the psalmist but are drawn from the covenant's own statement of what injustice deserves.

The specific episode is unknown. Readers have suggested the time of Doeg's betrayal in the court of Saul, 1 Samuel 22, or the slander of Absalom's faction, or the day Shimei cursed David as he fled Jerusalem, 2 Samuel 16:5 to 13. That last scene is a close parallel, since David refuses to silence Shimei and says, 'Perhaps the LORD will see my affliction and repay me with good for the cursing I receive today,' 2 Samuel 16:12. Verse 28 of the psalm says nearly the same: 'Though they curse, You will bless.'

The fasting of verse 24 and the head-shaking of verse 25 are further marks of a public humiliation. A person who fasted was seeking God, and onlookers who shook their heads signalled mockery, as in Psalm 22:7 and Lamentations 2:15.
context.canonical:
Psalm 109 belongs with the imprecatory psalms, those that call down judgment on enemies. Others in this group include Psalms 35, 58, 69, 83 and 137. Of these, Psalm 109 is the most concentrated, and its closest relation is Psalm 69. Peter, in Acts 1:20, quotes the two together, joining 'May his place be deserted,' from Psalm 69:25, with 'May another take his position,' from Psalm 109:8, to explain the fate of Judas. This is one of the few places where the New Testament draws on imprecatory psalms in a direct application.

The psalm also stands at a hinge in the book. It follows Psalm 108's confident prayer for victory and precedes Psalm 110, the oracle in which the Lord says to David's Lord, 'Sit at My right hand,' Psalm 110:1. The 'right hand' of Psalm 109:6 and 109:31 is therefore picked up at once by the next psalm. The needy man for whom God stands at the right hand in 109 is succeeded in 110 by the king who sits there.

The accuser at the right hand is a figure that reappears. In Zechariah 3:1 the satan stands at the right hand of Joshua the high priest 'to accuse him,' and is rebuked by the LORD. Job 1 and 2 show the satan presenting accusations before God. In Revelation 12:10 he is 'the accuser of our brothers,' who is thrown down. The Psalter's phrase for an enemy at one's right hand in court is thus the Bible's pattern for the work of the great adversary.

The theme of a righteous sufferer forced to bring his case to God also links this psalm to the passion of Jesus. The shaking of heads in verse 25 is what bystanders did at the cross, Matthew 27:39, and the pattern of love repaid with hatred, verses 4 and 5, was also Christ's experience. Yet the New Testament does not simply carry over the curses. It sets alongside them Jesus' command to love enemies, Luke 6:27, and His prayer on the cross, Luke 23:34, and asks the reader to hold both.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalm was written so that the wronged would know what to do with their anger. David does not deny that he is furious, and he does not take his own revenge. He names the lies, lists the injuries, and then hands the whole case to the one court that cannot be bought. The long curse of verses 6 to 19 is the shape that anger takes when it is placed in front of God, and it is bound by two facts: it is addressed to the LORD, not to the enemy, and it asks for a result that matches the offence, the man who loved cursing is to be wrapped in it, verses 17 to 19.

He also meant his hearers to see why the curse is justified. Verse 16 gives the charge: the man never thought to show kindness and pursued the poor and brokenhearted 'even to their death.' It is a charge of murder by oppression. By setting the offence in the centre, the psalmist makes the prayer a plea for justice for the vulnerable more than a private grudge.

Finally he meant to show where the speaker's confidence lies. Verses 21 and 26 base the plea on God's chesed, not David's innocence, though he claims innocence of the specific charge in verse 4. The poem ends with praise and a promise that the LORD stands with the needy. The hearer who prays it is meant to leave the court with the matter in God's hands and a song on his lips.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm records a prayer; it does not command believers to curse their enemies. The words are David's, and the New Testament places them inside a larger frame. Jesus taught His followers to love their enemies and pray for those who persecute them, Matthew 5:44, and Paul says, 'Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God's wrath,' Romans 12:19. Stephen dies praying for his killers, Acts 7:60, as Jesus had, Luke 23:34. A believer who reads Psalm 109 as permission to wish disaster on a neighbour has misread both the psalm and the Lord who is its fulfilment.

The prescriptive core is more modest and still demanding. It tells us not to keep silent about injustice before God, to give up private revenge, and to appeal to God as the judge of the earth. It also teaches that the Lord is a God who hears the accused. Verses 6 to 19 can be prayed in the Spirit of the New Testament as a plea against the powers of evil, Ephesians 6:12, and for the final righting of wrongs, Revelation 6:10, while we pray for our personal enemies as Jesus did.

The curse on children and descendants in verses 9 to 15 is the hardest part. These verses describe the logic of covenant justice in the ancient world, in which a family shared the fate of its head. They are not a rule for how any court should act, and the law itself forbids putting children to death for their fathers' sins, Deuteronomy 24:16. The sensible approach is to hear them as the cry of the wronged for a justice that completes itself, and then to bring them under the cross.

debates.question: Are verses 6 to 19 David's curse on his enemy, or his quotation of what the enemies say against him?

views.label: The curse is David's own prayer
views.case: Nothing in the text marks a change of speaker. Verse 20 closes the section with 'May this be the LORD's reward to my accusers,' which treats the preceding verses as the speaker's request. Peter treats verse 8 as Scripture spoken by the Holy Spirit through David concerning Judas, Acts 1:16 and 20. The sudden shift from the plural enemies of verses 1 to 5 to a single 'he' in verses 6 to 19 can be explained as the focus on the ringleader.

views.label: The curse is a quotation of the enemies' words
views.case: Some interpreters note that David has just said the enemies speak lies and curse, verses 2 and 3, and that the singular 'him' of verse 6 could be David himself, the target of their curse. On this reading verses 6 to 19 are the enemy's words, 'They say: Set over him a wicked man,' and the speaker's own prayer begins with verse 20. The proposal would soften the psalm's severity.

debates.bearing: The first view is better supported by the flow of the poem and by Acts 1:20, and the second is driven chiefly by the difficulty of the content. Even if the second were right, the psalm would still contain the strong imprecation of verses 17 to 19. The more helpful point is that verses 6 to 19 show anger voiced in prayer and not in action.

debates.question: How can a Christian pray an imprecatory psalm, given the call to love enemies?

views.label: They belong to an earlier stage and are set aside
views.case: Under the old covenant, justice was worked out in the nation, and prayers for the downfall of the wicked fit that setting. Jesus' Sermon on the Mount and Paul's instruction to bless those who persecute us, Romans 12:14, replace this posture for the church.

views.label: They are prayed as appeals for God's justice and not as personal hatred
views.case: The psalm gives vengeance to God and refuses to take it. It is a case of handing over, which is what Romans 12:19 also asks. The prayer for justice is also made by martyrs under the altar in Revelation 6:10. On this view the psalm teaches believers to put their anger in the hands of God.

views.label: They are heard as the voice of Christ and the righteous sufferer
views.case: Because the New Testament applies Psalm 109 to Judas and treats David's sufferings as pointing to Christ, the curses can be read as the words of the Anointed One against the powers that destroy the weak. Believers then pray them with Him, against spiritual evil and for the final victory over injustice.

debates.bearing: These views are not mutually exclusive. The church has long prayed the psalm in its second and third senses, while holding with Jesus that our personal enemies are to be loved. The psalm should never be used to justify revenge, but it should also not be skipped, because it teaches honesty with God about evil.

study.originalLanguages:
The most important word is satan in verse 6. In Hebrew it is first a common noun for an adversary or accuser, and it comes from a verb meaning to oppose or accuse. That verb is the one in verse 4, where the speaker says 'they accuse me,' and the participle appears again in verses 20 and 29 of his 'accusers.' When the title with the definite article is used, as in Job 1 and Zechariah 3:1, it names the heavenly accuser. Here there is no article, and the word may be read simply as 'an accuser.' The psalm's argument is that the practice of accusing, which the enemies use against the innocent, is turned against the one who began it.

In verse 4 the speaker says, 'but I am a man of prayer.' The Hebrew is shorter and stranger: 'but I, prayer.' The BSB rightly supplies 'a man of,' but the original makes the speaker's whole self into a prayer. When the enemies accuse, he does not argue back; he becomes an offering to God. The same noun appears in the next sentence of verse 7, where the enemy's prayer is to be counted as sin, so that two prayers, one of the innocent and one of the guilty, are set in contrast. Proverbs 28:9 teaches that the prayer of the one who turns from the law is detestable.

The verb in verse 6, 'set over him,' comes from the root paqad, which means to appoint or to attend to. The same root gives the noun in verse 8 translated 'position,' pequddah, the office of oversight. In Acts 1:20 Peter quotes the Greek form of this line, using the word for the office of an overseer, which is why he applies it to the vacated apostolic post. The footnote on verse 8 simply notes that the verse is cited in Acts 1:20.

Verse 17 sets two pairs side by side: the enemy loved cursing and refused to delight in blessing. The Hebrew verbs are ahav, to love, and chafets, to delight. These are the language of covenant loyalty, and the verses suggest that he chose cursing as a way of life. Hence the justice of verses 18 and 19: he put on the cursing as a garment, and the prayer is that he will have to wear it. The footnote for verse 10 notes that the Hebrew reads 'seek' while the Septuagint may read 'be driven out,' a small variant that does not change the picture of destitution.

The speaker's self-description in verse 23 uses two images that do not translate smoothly: 'a lengthening shadow' and a locust that is 'shaken off.' A shadow that stretches is about to vanish at sunset, and a locust shaken from a garment is driven away without mercy. Both describe a life draining away.

The last verse reverses the opening of the curse. In verse 31, 'He stands at the right hand of the needy one,' the word for needy, evyon, is the one used of the victims in verse 16 and of the speaker in verse 22. The 'condemners of his soul' are literally those who judge his life. The psalm began with the request 'be not silent,' and it ends with a God who stands up.

typology.type: The falsely accused righteous man, verses 2 to 5
typology.fulfillment: David is hated for his love and answers with prayer. Jesus stands before the Sanhedrin and Pilate, accused by false witnesses, Matthew 26:59 to 61, and answers with silence and trust, 1 Peter 2:23. The escalation is that David's innocence was only relative, while Christ is without sin, 1 Peter 2:22. The type falls short in the prayer itself: David asks God for judgment on his enemies, while Christ asks the Father to forgive them, Luke 23:34.

typology.type: The accuser at the right hand, verses 6 and 31
typology.fulfillment: The Hebrew accuser stands at the right hand of the guilty, and the LORD stands at the right hand of the needy. In Zechariah 3:1 the satan accuses Joshua and is rebuked. In the New Testament the one who is at the right hand of God is Christ, who intercedes for us, Romans 8:34, and Stephen sees Him standing there, Acts 7:55. The accuser of our brothers is thrown down, Revelation 12:10. The type falls short because the psalm pictures a single court case; the New Testament reveals a cosmic one with a final verdict.

Peter applies 'May another take his position' to Judas, whose place among the Twelve was filled by Matthias, Acts 1:20 to 26. The pattern is that a betrayer of God's anointed loses his office. The escalation is that the one betrayed is the true Son of David, and the betrayal was within the plan of God, Acts 2:23. It is also noted that the quotation is joined with Psalm 69:25, so Peter is applying a pair of psalms and not forcing a single verse. The type falls short because Judas is the only person to whom the New Testament applies the verse.

The speaker's love is met with evil. Jesus says that the world hated Him, John 15:18, and John applies the 'without cause' language of other psalms to Him, John 15:25. On the cross He prays for those who hate Him. The escalation is that the Son loves to the end, John 13:1, and bears the penalty of those who return evil for good. The type falls short because David's love was imperfect and he still wished for judgment.

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ first as the pattern of the innocent sufferer. David describes a man who loves and prays and is accused. 'In return for my love they accuse me, but I am a man of prayer,' verse 4. In the Gospels, the scene is the same, but far deeper. Jesus loved the people who handed Him over, healed the servant whose ear was cut off, Luke 22:51, and prayed for those who drove in the nails, Luke 23:34. The accusation, 'hatred for my love,' verse 5, is the text of the passion. Yet He did not answer in kind: 'When they hurled insults at Him, He did not retaliate; when He suffered, He made no threats. Instead, He entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly,' 1 Peter 2:23. The psalm's strategy of handing the case to God is carried out perfectly.

It leads to Christ through the apostolic use of verse 8. Peter says the Holy Spirit foretold through David the fate of Judas, Acts 1:16, and quotes verse 8 for the replacement of his office. This makes it plain that the first Christians read the psalm as a witness to the betrayal of the Messiah. The betrayer who 'pursued the poor and needy' becomes the one who sold the Poor Man for silver. It also means that the severe parts of the psalm are not simply hatred but judgment on the one who opposes God's anointed.

It leads to Christ in the right-hand imagery. The psalm opens with an accuser at the right hand of the guilty and ends with the LORD at the right hand of the needy. The next psalm sets the Messiah at God's right hand, Psalm 110:1, and the New Testament shows Him there. Stephen, as the accusing crowd gnashes its teeth, sees Jesus standing at the right hand of God, Acts 7:55, which is the posture of an advocate rising to speak. Paul asks, 'Who is there to condemn us?' and answers that Christ Jesus is at the right hand of God, interceding for us, Romans 8:34, which is the final word on the 'condemners of his soul' in verse 31. And John writes that we have an Advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the Righteous One, 1 John 2:1. The accuser who prosecutes day and night has been thrown down, Revelation 12:10.

It leads to Christ through the contrast between the curse and the cross. The enemy in the psalm loved cursing and it was to be wrapped around him. On the cross Christ became a curse for us, Galatians 3:13, taking on Himself the cursing that belonged to His accusers, and wearing it so that we might wear the robe of righteousness instead, Isaiah 61:10. The garment imagery of verses 18, 19 and 29 is thus transformed: the shame that others were to wear Christ wore for them.

A caution is needed. The psalm does not predict Jesus in every line, and the curses against the family of the accuser should not be read as aimed at anyone's family today. The fulfillment lies in the pattern of the righteous sufferer, the specific New Testament use of verse 8, and the picture of the God who stands with the needy.
study.god:
The psalm begins by calling God 'the God of my praise,' and ends by praising Him in the presence of many, so that praise is both the ground and the goal of the prayer. The phrase echoes Deuteronomy 10:21, 'He is your praise and He is your God.' The God of the psalm is not a means to winning an argument; He is the one whom the speaker wants to be known and honoured for what He does. The cry 'be not silent' is a cry of faith, since only someone who believes God can speak can be troubled that He seems not to.

God is the Judge who hears the accused. The whole poem is addressed to Him, and nothing is said to the enemy. This tells us that He is open to complaint. The ancient world had gods who were silent or capricious, and Israel's God is the one who can be addressed as a Judge about wrongs. He is also the Judge who can be trusted with the work of retribution because He is just. The curse that gives each person what he has given, the cursing he loved falling on him, verse 17, is the law of the covenant: the deeds of a person return upon him, Psalm 7:15 and 16, Proverbs 26:27.

He is a God who defends the weak. The accused man calls himself 'poor and needy' twice, verses 22 and 31, and the same words describe the people the wicked man hunted. The psalm closes with the statement that the LORD stands at the right hand of such a man. That is God's own pattern. He is 'a father to the fatherless and a champion of widows,' Psalm 68:5, and the covenant says He will hear their cry, Exodus 22:23. The curse of fatherless children in verse 9 is not a delight in suffering but the law's own warning that those who orphan others will know the same.

He is a God of chesed. The speaker does not argue from merit, and in both verse 21 and verse 26 his appeal is to God's loving devotion. The point is that the speaker cannot guarantee his own cause, but he can count on God's character. 'For the sake of Your name' in verse 21 brings the same ground. God's reputation is bound up with the rescue of those who trust Him.

He is a God who answers cursing with blessing. 'Though they curse, You will bless.' The statement is as bold as the earlier imprecation, and it echoes the covenant promise to Abraham, Genesis 12:3, where blessing and cursing are God's to give. The psalm wagers that God's word of blessing is stronger than any human word of curse.

For worship, the psalm teaches that anger can be turned into prayer and prayer into praise. A believer who has been wronged is invited to bring the whole story to God, with its bitterness and its detail, and to leave it there. The final lines show that this practice is not wasted: the person who began in complaint ends with a vow to thank the LORD 'profusely' in front of others, and with confidence that the one who stands at the side of the needy will save him.

crossReferences.note: Shimei curses David as he flees. David refuses to silence him and says the LORD may repay him with good for the cursing. It is the nearest narrative parallel to verses 28 and 29, and it shows how David could pray fiercely and yet refuse to take revenge himself.

A false witness is to be given the penalty he intended for his brother. The law supplies the principle behind verses 6 to 7 and 17 to 19: the harm planned for another is to return upon the one who planned it, and it is given to judges and not to individuals.

God warns that if anyone mistreats widows and orphans He will hear their cry and make the oppressor's wives widows and his children fatherless. This is the source of the imagery in verses 9 and 10, and shows the curses are drawn from the covenant itself.

The satan stands at the right hand of Joshua the high priest to accuse him, and the LORD rebukes him. It is the closest picture of the scene in verse 6, and it shows God not siding with the accuser but with the one accused.

Another prayer of the righteous sufferer, with similar curses. Peter combines verse 25 of this psalm with Psalm 109:8 in Acts 1:20, so the two psalms are read as a pair about the betrayer of the Messiah.

Peter explains Judas' fate and the choice of Matthias by quoting Psalm 69 and Psalm 109:8. It is the key New Testament use of this psalm, and it shows that the early church read David's words as the voice of the Spirit about the betrayal of Jesus.

Jesus tells His disciples to love their enemies and pray for those who persecute them. It stands beside the psalm as the necessary counterpart. The psalm shows honest anger brought to God, and Jesus shows how that anger is taken up into love.

On the cross Jesus prays, 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.' Set against verses 6 to 19, it shows the difference between the king who calls for judgment and the King who bears it, and it marks the point where imprecation gives way to forgiveness.

Paul asks who will bring a charge or condemn, and answers that Christ is at the right hand of God interceding. It is the gospel answer to the 'condemners of his soul' in verse 31, and it moves the psalm's last image from hope to accomplished fact.

Paul forbids repaying evil for evil and tells believers to leave room for God's wrath. It states the discipline the psalm models in its own way, bringing vengeance to God, and adds the call to overcome evil with good.

Stephen, accused by false witnesses, sees Jesus standing at the right hand of God, and dies praying for his killers. It shows the psalm's last verse in action: the Lord stands with the accused, and the accused prays as his Lord did.

The accuser of our brothers, who accuses them day and night, is thrown down. It brings the psalm's accuser to his end and shows that the charges laid against God's people are finally silenced by the victory of Christ.

study.oneStory:
The psalm sits within the biggest question of the Bible: what will God do about evil? From Genesis 3 the world has a tempter and accuser who lies, who first questions God's word and then tells humans they are condemned. The story of the Bible is the story of how God deals with that accuser. Abel's blood cries out from the ground, Genesis 4:10, and God hears. The law provides courts, witnesses and penalties so that injustice may be answered, and the Psalms give the wronged a voice before the highest court. Psalm 109 is the most concentrated of those voices, a cry from someone whose accusers have the crowd but who has appealed over their heads.

What the psalm sets up is the question of how the accused can be vindicated and the accuser silenced without God becoming unjust Himself. If God simply dismisses the charges, He seems to overlook sin. If He sentences the accused, He abandons the needy. The Old Testament holds this tension with a promise: the LORD will stand at the right hand of the needy, and the accuser will be rebuked. The prophets make the promise more precise by picturing a servant who is accused and killed, and yet who bears the sins of many and is vindicated, Isaiah 53:3 to 12.

In Christ the tension is resolved. The accuser at the right hand of the guilty has real material for his charges, and the Son of God takes the penalty on Himself, so that the accuser has nothing left to say. The cross is where the curse of the law is borne, Galatians 3:13, and the resurrection is the verdict that the accused one is righteous. Christ at the right hand of God is the end of condemnation, Romans 8:1 and 34. The betrayer of the Messiah is judged, as the psalm said, and the apostles are given another to take his place, Acts 1:20. The church lives under the new commandment to love enemies, and yet it still prays for justice, as the martyrs do in Revelation 6:10.

The new creation is the place where the psalm's prayers are finally answered. The accuser is thrown down, Revelation 12:10, and cast into the lake of fire, Revelation 20:10. God's people no longer need to defend themselves, for He wipes away every tear, Revelation 21:4, and nothing accursed will be found any longer, Revelation 22:3. The clothing imagery is fulfilled: the redeemed wear white robes washed in the blood of the Lamb, Revelation 7:14, rather than shame. The needy one who was once surrounded by accusers has become a member of a people who see God's face and who sing, 'Salvation belongs to our God,' Revelation 7:10.

quiz.q: How does David describe the treatment he has received from his accusers in verses 4-5?

options.text: They repay his love with accusation and hatred, evil for good.
options.note: This stark reversal, love met with hatred, is the wound that drives the entire psalm.

options.text: They ignore him completely and say nothing against him.
options.note: The opposite is true; wicked and deceitful mouths actively speak against him.

options.text: They repay his kindness with equal kindness.
options.note: David explicitly says evil for good, hatred for love, not reciprocated kindness.

options.text: They only oppose him in private, never publicly.
options.note: The text does not limit the accusation to private settings; it describes open, surrounding hostility.

quiz.q: What does David do instead of taking revenge himself against his accuser?

options.text: He hands the case entirely to God in prayer, asking the righteous Judge to act.
options.note: The entire imprecation, verses 6-20, is addressed to God, not carried out by David's own hand.

options.text: He organizes his own supporters to retaliate.
options.note: David takes no such action; the psalm is entirely a prayer, not a plan of retaliation.

options.text: He quietly accepts the slander without any response.
options.note: David responds vigorously in prayer, though not through the accepted silence this option suggests.

options.text: He appeals to the king's court for a legal ruling.
options.note: His appeal is to God directly, described in legal imagery, but the court is heavenly, not an earthly tribunal.

quiz.q: What is David's only stated ground for rescue in verses 21 and 26?

options.text: God's loving devotion, His chesed, not David's own merit.
options.note: Both verses appeal explicitly to God's steadfast love as the sole basis for deliverance.

options.text: David's flawless righteousness and good record.
options.note: David appeals to God's character, not his own merit, as the ground for rescue.

options.text: The number of allies David has gathered.
options.note: The psalm shows David isolated and scorned, not surrounded by supportive allies.

options.text: His wealth and social status.
options.note: David describes himself as poor and needy, the opposite of relying on wealth or status.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament apply verse 8 of this psalm?

options.text: Peter applies it to Judas Iscariot and the filling of his apostolic office by Matthias.
options.note: Acts 1:20 quotes this verse directly regarding Judas' betrayal and replacement.

options.text: It is never referenced anywhere in the New Testament.
options.note: Acts 1:20 quotes this very verse directly.

options.text: Paul applies it generally to all false teachers in Galatia.
options.note: The specific New Testament application is to Judas in Acts 1, not a general reference in Galatians.

options.text: It is applied to the Roman soldiers who crucified Jesus.
options.note: The specific apostolic application is to Judas' betrayal and office, not the soldiers at the cross.

quiz.q: How does Christ ultimately go beyond this psalm's pattern of entrusting judgment to God?

options.text: Though reviled, He did not revile in return, and even prayed for His executioners' forgiveness.
options.note: 1 Peter 2:23 and Luke 23:34 show Christ both entrusting Himself to the Father and actively praying mercy for His accusers.

options.text: He personally cursed every one of His accusers by name.
options.note: Christ's response was forgiveness and entrustment to the Father, not personal cursing.

options.text: He avoided the false accusations by fleeing Jerusalem.
options.note: Christ did not flee; He submitted to false accusation and crucifixion.

options.text: He demanded that Pilate immediately punish His accusers.
options.note: Christ made no such demand; He entrusted Himself to the Father who judges justly.

questions: David is repaid evil for the good and love he showed others. Where have you experienced this kind of unjust reversal, and how did you respond?
Instead of taking revenge, David hands his entire case to God in prayer. What would it look like to fully surrender a desire for payback to God this week rather than acting on it yourself?
David's only appeal for rescue is God's loving devotion, not his own merit. Are you tempted to believe God owes you help because of your own goodness, rather than resting on His grace alone?

This psalm's harshest words are ultimately read by the apostles as pointing to Judas, the betrayer of the true King. How does seeing God's justice reach even to Christ's betrayer strengthen your trust that no injustice done to you is finally hidden from Him?

Christ, unlike the imprecation of this psalm, prayed forgiveness for His accusers even while suffering. Where is God calling you to move from merely trusting Him with justice toward also actively forgiving those who have wronged you?

translationNotes.note: Accuser renders the Hebrew satan, a legal adversary who stood at a defendant's side in ancient courts; David asks that this role be turned back on the one who has falsely accused him.
May another take his position is quoted in Acts 1:20 concerning the office vacated by Judas Iscariot and filled by Matthias.

The Hebrew text reads seeking sustenance, while the ancient Greek Septuagint reads may they be driven, a minor textual variant that does not change the verse's picture of the wicked man's family reduced to homeless want.
